findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so the claimed 'natural backpressure' does not exist and the consumer can OOM
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates plain `queue.Queue()` instances with no maxsize, and `submit()` calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` which never blocks. If processing is slower than consumption (the exact scenario this PR is designed to address — one slow item per queue), the queues grow without bound in memory, since the arroyo consumer keeps polling and submitting messages. The docstring on SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false. The consumer will buffer the entire topic backlog in-process and can be OOM-killed. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) so that `put` blocks the submit thread and actually applies backpressure.

findings.title: FixedQueuePool is shut down permanently on strategy close, breaking the consumer after any partition rebalance
findings.body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates the FixedQueuePool once in `__init__` (result_consumer.py line 133), and every call to `create_with_partitions` builds a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy wrapping that same pool. When partitions are revoked (rebalance), arroyo calls `close()` on the old strategy, which calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` — and `queue.Queue.shutdown()` is irreversible, plus `worker.shutdown = True` permanently stops the worker threads. On the next `create_with_partitions` after reassignment, the new strategy submits to shut-down queues whose workers have exited: messages will be accepted by `submit` (or raise `queue.ShutDown` from `put`) but never processed, stalling the consumer indefinitely with no errors. The pool must be created per-partition-assignment (in `create_with_partitions`) or restartable.

findings.title: close() stops the commit thread before workers finish draining, so processed offsets are never committed
findings.body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close(), the shutdown event is set and the commit thread is joined first, and only then is the queue pool shut down to drain. Any offsets completed by workers after the commit thread exits are never committed, and there is no final commit pass after the pool drains. On every shutdown/rebalance this silently reprocesses up to the last second-plus of already-handled messages; more importantly the pool's `worker.shutdown = True` flags mean items still sitting in the queues are dropped from memory entirely without their offsets ever being completed or committed. A graceful close should drain the queues, then run one final commit of get_committable_offsets() before joining the commit thread.

findings.title: OffsetTracker retains offsets for revoked partitions forever and the commit loop may commit offsets for partitions the consumer no longer owns
findings.body: OffsetTracker never removes entries for partitions that are revoked during a rebalance — `all_offsets`/`outstanding`/`last_committed` grow monotonically, and `_commit_loop` keeps calling `commit_function` (which is arroyo's commit callback for the current assignment) with committable offsets for partitions the consumer may no longer own. Committing offsets for unassigned partitions is rejected by Kafka (or worse, commits a stale generation's offsets) and any remaining outstanding offset in a revoked partition will cause that partition to never advance in `get_committable_offsets`, keeping the tracker data alive forever. create_with_partitions/revocation should reset or prune per-partition tracking state.

findings.title: Factory shutdown() sets queue_pool to None while strategies still reference it, and double-shutdown of a queue.Queue raises
findings.body: ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and sets `self.queue_pool = None`, but any live SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy created by `create_with_partitions` still holds a reference to the pool and its `close()` will call `queue_pool.shutdown()` again. The second call invokes `queue.Queue.shutdown()` on an already-shut-down queue, which raises `queue.ShutDown`; the bare `except Exception` around `q.shutdown` in FixedQueuePool.swallows it, but the strategy's close ordering then becomes unpredictable. The factory and strategy both own pool lifecycle with no coordination — one of them should be responsible for shutdown.

findings.title: submit() swallows all exceptions including grouping/serialization bugs and silently marks the offset complete, dropping messages
findings.body: In SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit(), any exception from the decoder, `grouping_fn`, or `queue_pool.submit` is caught by the broad `except Exception` and the offset is added-then-completed, which makes it eligible to be committed. Unlike a decode failure (which legitimately returns None), a bug in `build_payload_grouping_key` or an internal error in pool submission now silently discards the message and commits past it with only a log line. For a Kafka consumer this converts transient/programming errors into permanent message loss rather than crashing or DLQ'ing. At minimum, non-decode failures should not mark the offset committable.

findings.title: test_stats_reporting asserts queue is non-empty immediately after submit, which is inherently flaky
findings.body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. Since the pool's worker threads start consuming as soon as items are enqueued, on a fast machine all 10 items can be processed before `get_stats()` runs, making this assertion fail nondeterministically. The same race applies to several uptime tests that poll `stats['total_items'] == 0 and call_count == N` — if a worker drains the queue before the mock records the call... actually those poll until a condition, so they are fine, but the immediate `> 0` assertion has no synchronization and will flake under load or with eager workers.
